title: 10 Disturbing Crimes in Arizona History
fullText: Number one, Judy Anne Arias. To understand what happened inside that bathroom in Mesa, you first have to understand a woman who could hold two completely different versions of herself in her mind at the same time and believe both. That more than the weapon, more than the timeline is the thread that runs through this entire case. Long before she was a defendant, Jodie Aras had already learned to edit reality until it fit the shape she needed it to take. She was born in July of 1980 in Salinas, California into a family that from the outside looked ordinary enough. Those who studied her later noted something that would matter a great deal. Even in her own accounts of her childhood, the facts seemed to bend depending on the audience. She described discipline in the home as harsh and at times abusive. Family members disputed the severity. What is significant is not which version was true, but that Jodi appeared able to summon whichever narrative served the moment. This is the emotional architecture that psychologists would later spend months trying to map. A personality that treated the truth as negotiable, something to be arranged rather than reported. As a young woman, she drifted. She left school before finishing, worked a series of jobs, moved between relationships, and developed a pattern that would repeat throughout her adult life. She became whoever the person in front of her wanted. Former partners described the same unsettling quality. When she loved someone, she did not simply love them. She dissolved into them, adopting their interests, their beliefs, their faith, their friends, remaking herself in their image with startling speed. To an insecure man, this could feel like devotion. To anyone watching from a distance, it looked like a self with no fixed center. Keep that quality in mind because it becomes far more important later. In 2006, she met Travis Alexander at a work conference in Las Vegas. He was ambitious, charismatic, deeply involved in his church and drawn to her. Within a short time, Jod converted to his faith. She relocated. She reorganized her life around proximity to him. The relationship, by the accounts of nearly everyone around them, was intense and unstable from the beginning. Passionate, then bitter, then passionate again. When they formally broke up, the romantic connection did not end so much as change form. And here the pattern that had defined her since childhood began to curdle into something dangerous. The self that had no center now had nowhere to anchor. Friends of Travis later said they had grown alarmed. They described Jodie appearing where she was not expected. They spoke of a growing sense that she could not accept the ending of things. What in an earlier relationship had looked like intense attachment now looked like something harder to name. a refusal to be released. She had reshaped herself entirely around this man. To lose him was not merely heartbreak. It was, in a very real psychological sense, the loss of the only self she currently had. On the 4th of June, 2008, she traveled a long distance by car to reach his home. What happened inside that house was, by the physical evidence, sudden and overwhelming. Travis was attacked in his bathroom and died from multiple stab wounds and a gunshot. Out of respect for him, the specific details are best left to the record. What matters for understanding Jod is what she did afterward because her behavior in the following days is a window directly into how her mind operated under pressure. She did not flee in panic. She did not confess. Instead, she began to build. Within days, she was leaving warm voicemails on Travis's phone, the phone of a man she knew was dead. She spoke to his friends as though nothing had happened. She continued a flirtation with another man and traveled to see him. She composed, in effect, a performance of innocence so complete that it suggested she had already begun rewriting the event in her own mind, reshaping it, as she had reshaped everything else into a version she could live inside. When investigators found Travis's body and the evidence began pointing toward her, the true test of that mind began. Her first version was simple. She was never there. She knew nothing. But police had recovered a camera from the scene. In the moments surrounding the attack, that camera had accidentally captured images, placing her unmistakably inside the house. Confronted with the impossible, most people crumble. Jod did something more revealing. She built a new story. Now, she admitted she had been there, but she claimed masked intruders had committed the killing while she fled in terror. It was a story with no supporting evidence and considerable contradicting evidence. It too collapsed, and so she built again. This third version would become the centerpiece of one of the most watched trials in American history, self-defense. She now testified that Travis had been abusive, that she had lived in fear, and that on that day she had defended her life. Crucially, she claimed she could not remember most of the killing itself. A defense expert testified that Jod suffered from post-traumatic stress and that a traumatic event could cause exactly that kind of memory gap. This is the psychological heart of the case. Three complete, mutually exclusive narratives, each delivered with apparent conviction. To many observers, the memory gap looked like the final most sophisticated edit. The mind erasing the one part of the story it could not safely narrate. Whether one saw calculated deception or genuine dissociation, the pattern was the same pattern that had defined her entire life. Reality rearranged to serve survival. The trial in Phoenix stretched across months in 2013 and became a national spectacle. Jod testified for 18 days. She was calm, articulate, and to the prosecution chilling in her composure. She sketched drawings in the courtroom. She gave a television interview minutes after her own conviction. Prosecutor Juan Martinez pressed her relentlessly on the contradictions between her stories, and the jury watched a woman who seemed genuinely unable to understand why holding three irreconcilable truths should trouble anyone. She was convicted of first-degree murder. The penalty phase deadlocked, two separate juries could not unanimously agree on death, and she was ultimately sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of release. She remains incarcerated in Arizona. What lingers about Jodi Ararius is not the violence alone. It is the quieter, stranger thing beneath it. A person who appeared to have built her identity entirely out of other people, and who, when the last of those people was taken away, seemed willing to construct any reality at all, rather than face the emptiness underneath. The most disturbing possibility raised by her case was never whether she lied. It was whether in some measure she had convinced herself. Number two, Mark Gudo. The most frightening thing about the man Phoenix came to call the baseline killer was not that he hunted strangers in the dark. It was that by day he was reportedly the kind of neighbor who would help you carry groceries. A married man employed, quiet, unremarkable to nearly everyone who crossed his path. To trace his mind is to confront a disturbing truth that predatory violence does not always announce itself and can live for years behind an ordinary face. Mark Gudo was born in September of 1964 in Phoenix, Arizona into a large family. Accounts of his upbringing describe hardship and instability, the kind of environment that appears again and again in the histories of violent offenders. Though it must be said plainly that the overwhelming majority of people from difficult childhoods never harm anyone. What separates a life like his is not simply adversity. It is what a particular mind does with resentment, opportunity, and the absence of empathy. And in Gudo's history, the warning signs accumulated long before the killings began. He had prior encounters with the law and a documented record of violence in his younger years. But he served time, was released, and re-entered ordinary life. He married to those around him. He seemed to have turned a corner. His wife, throughout everything that followed, publicly defended him and insisted on his innocence. This is part of what makes the case so unsettling from a psychological standpoint. The domestic normaly was not a thin disguise hastily assembled. It was a durable, functioning second life. He was in the clinical sense capable of compartmentalization so complete that the two halves of his existence never appeared to touch. That compartmentalization is the key to understanding the terror he unleashed between the summer of 2005 and the summer of 2006. During that year, the Phoenix area was gripped by two separate waves of fear at once. the random shootings of the serial shooter case which we will come to and a second entirely different predator. This second offender did not fire from moving cars. He approached his victims directly on the street in parking lots near their homes. He was armed, he robbed, he committed sexual assaults and he killed. Over the course of that year, nine people lost their lives to him and many more were assaulted or terrorized. Because several early attacks occurred along Baseline Road, the press gave him the name that would stick. The psychological profile that emerged during the investigation described a man driven by control and domination rather than by any single simple motive. The attacks were not impulsive outbursts. They showed planning, mobility, and a chilling adaptability. He altered his appearance. He struck across a wide geographic area, which made the pattern harder to see. For months, the region lived under a kind of collective dread, with residents changing their routines, avoiding being alone outdoors, and watching strangers with new suspicion. To understand what he did, you have to stay with how he was operating beneath the surface because the ordinariness was not incidental to the crimes. It was the engine that allowed them to continue. Each time he returned home to a normal domestic life, he reset. The absence of any visible disturbance in his daily behavior meant that nothing around him raised an alarm. This is the terrible efficiency of a certain kind of offender. the better they are at appearing harmless, the longer they remain free. His undoing came through evidence, not confession. During one of the earlier assaults, before the full pattern was understood, biological evidence had been recovered. When Gudau was eventually identified as a suspect through other channels, and that evidence was compared, the match was, according to the prosecution, powerful. DNA became the thread that connected the ordinary neighbor to the shadow that had haunted the city. It is a reminder of how modern the resolution of this case truly was. That the science, more than any eyewitness, is what finally pierced the disguise. He was arrested in September of 2006. The relief across Phoenix was immense, but so was the disbelief among those who knew him. The gap between the man they thought they knew and the man described in the charges was almost impossible for many to reconcile. That gap is in the end the psychological center of the entire story. His prosecution unfolded in stages. He was first tried and convicted in connection with an assault on two sisters, one of whom was pregnant. Then came the far larger case. In 2011, a Maricopa County jury convicted Mark Gudau on dozens of counts spanning the full series of crimes, and he was sentenced to death for the nine murders. He was sent to Arizona's death row, where he remains, and where his legal team has continued to file appeals, including claims disputing the evidence against him. What his case left behind was more than a resolved investigation. It left a lasting lesson embedded in the psychology of an entire community. The knowledge that danger does not always look like danger and that the most effective predators are often the ones who are easiest to overlook. The baseline killer taught Phoenix to distrust the comfort of the familiar face and that is a wound that does not fully close. Number three, Dale Shaner. Some killers are driven by rage, some by compulsion, some by delusion. Dale Hner belonged to a rarer and colder category. A man who appears to have killed for the sensation of it, treating human lives as targets in a game only he was playing. To sit with his psychology is to confront the unsettling possibility of violence without any conventional motive at all. Violence pursued the way another person might pursue a hobby. He was born in 1973 and by the accounts that emerged later, his adult life was marked by a series of quiet failures and disappointments. He had worked various jobs, including at a Phoenix airport. He had experienced the collapse of relationships and the loss of custody arrangements involving his children. He suffered by some descriptions from depression and a corrosive sense that his life had amounted to nothing. None of that is unusual. Millions of people carry disappointment. What makes Howner's case a genuine psychological autopsy is the way that ordinary despair curdled in his particular mind into a hunger for control expressed through random destruction. That hunger did not begin with murder. It began, investigators later concluded, with fire and with smaller cruelties. There were arson. There were attacks on animals. And then escalating through 2005 and into 2006, it became attacks on people, strangers chosen for no reason other than that they happened to be walking, cycling, or standing alone at night in the Phoenix area. The method was drive by shooting. The victims were random. There was no connection between them. No shared characteristic that could help investigators predict where the next attack would come. This randomness was itself a form of terror. A city can guard against a threat with a pattern. It cannot easily guard against a shadow that strikes anyone anywhere for nothing. Over the span of the shooting spree, six people were killed and many more were wounded alongside the shootings of animals and acts of arson that formed the wider pattern of destruction. Howner did not act entirely alone during the peak of the violence. He had an accomplice, a man named Samuel Dyman, whose story appears later in this list. But the investigation and the courts identified Howner as the driving force, the one whose fixation propelled the spree. What the psychological record suggests is that the shootings gave Howner something his failing life had denied him. A sense of power, of consequence, of being the author of events rather than their victim. In the most disturbing sense, the terror he created was, for him, a kind of achievement. His capture came not through forensics alone, but through human weakness in his own circle. His accomplice talked, drawn out in part by an acquaintance who grew suspicious and cooperated with police. Surveillance followed. The pieces came together, and in August of 2006, the arrests were made. When police searched and pieced through the evidence, a picture emerged of a man who had in effect been documenting his own reign of fear, collecting, tracking, following the news coverage of the attacks he had committed. That detail is central to understanding him. He was not hiding from the story. He was consuming it. He wanted to see the effect he was having. His trial in 2009 laid the full pattern before a jury and it was overwhelming. Dale Hner was convicted of six murders and dozens of additional counts and he was sentenced to death. But the final chapter of his story is in its own way the most revealing. On death row, Howner did something that stunned observers. He asked the courts to stop his appeals and to allow his execution to proceed. He wanted it over. He never reached the execution chamber. In 2013, Dale Howner was found dead in his cell, having taken his own life. The man who had treated the lives of strangers as disposable had, in the end, disposed of his own. What his case leaves behind is a difficult meditation on the emptiness at the core of certain kinds of violence. There was no grand grievance, no coherent cause, no explanation that could give the victim's families the comfort of a reason. There was only a man whose interior life had collapsed into a void, and who tried to fill that void by inflicting fear on people who had never done anything to him. Phoenix survived his summer of terror, but the randomness of it left a particular kind of scar. The knowledge that some dangers cannot be reasoned with only stopped number four, Winnie Ruth Jud. She was 26 years old, small, soft-spoken, employed as a medical secretary, and she would spend the rest of her long life as a figure of national fascination. Because the woman at the center of the trunk murders may have been all at once a killer, a victim of a broken mind, and a person the justice system of her era never truly understood. To examine Winnie Ruth Jud is to examine how mental illness, gender, and the crude psychiatry of the 1930s collided in a single sensational case. She was born in 1899 in Indiana, the daughter of a minister. As a young woman, she married a physician considerably older than herself, and her life was marked from early on by illness, instability, and periods of profound emotional distress. She struggled with her health, both physical and mental, in ways that the medicine of her time was illquipped to address. When she moved to Phoenix in the early 1930s, she was a young woman already carrying a fragile psychological state into a new and unfamiliar life. In Phoenix, she made friends, two women in particular, with whom she shared a close social circle. On a hot October night in 1931, those two friendships ended in violence. Both women were shot and killed. What happened in the hours and days that followed turned a local tragedy into one of the most bizarre criminal spectacles of the century. The bodies were placed into trunks. Those trunks were then transported by train from Phoenix to Los Angeles. When Jud arrived to claim them, and the baggage agents grew suspicious of a foul odor and leaking fluid, the horror was discovered. The press seized upon the story instantly, and she became known across the country as the trunk murderous or the velvet tigress. Lurid names for a case whose actual facts were far murkier and sadder than the headlines suggested. Here the psychological questions crowded in, and they were never fully resolved. Jud's own account was that a confrontation had occurred, that a struggle over a weapon had taken place, and that she had acted in self-defense during a violent argument. The physical evidence and the dismemberment that followed painted a darker and more disturbing picture that was difficult to square with a simple story of self-p protection. But layered over all of it was the undeniable reality of her deteriorating mental state. a woman whose grip on stability had been precarious for years and who by any measure was not psychologically well. She was tried and convicted of murder and sentenced to death. And then the case took the turn that would define the rest of her life. Before the sentence could be carried out, she was examined and found mentally incompetent. The execution was set aside and instead of the gallows, Winnie Ruth Jud was committed to the Arizona State Asylum for the Insane. What followed was extraordinary. Over the next several decades, Jud escaped from the institution again and again by various counts six or seven times. She would vanish, sometimes for extended periods, once living for years under an assumed name and working quietly as a housekeeper before being recognized and returned. These escapes made her a folk figure, half monster and half something else in the public imagination. A woman who could not be contained by the institution meant to hold her to read her story through a modern lens is to see a case that would almost certainly be handled entirely differently today. The overlapping questions of severe mental illness, the trauma and instability of her earlier life, and the primitive psychiatric standards of the era combined to produce a resolution that satisfied no one and clarified little. Was she a calculating killer? Was she a profoundly ill woman who committed a terrible act in a state of crisis? The honest answer nearly a century later is that the full truth is buried in a time whose understanding of the human mind was still crude. She was eventually granted parole in the early 1970s, an old woman by then, and she lived quietly for many years afterward, dying in 1998 at the age of 98. Her life had spanned nearly the entire 20th century, and for most of it she carried a name that the public had reduced to a headline. What endures about Winnie Ruth Jud is the discomfort her case still provokes. It resists the clean categories that true crime prefers. It asks us to hold together the reality of two women who died, and the reality of a killer whose own mind was, by the standards of any era, deeply broken. Her story is a reminder that justice and understanding are not always the same thing and that some cases leave us with more questions than the law was ever built to answer. Number five, Wendy Elizabeth Andriano. There is a particular kind of case that unsettles people more than the crimes of strangers, and it is the case of the caregiver who kills the person she was trusted to protect. Wendy Andreano was to her neighbors in the quiet suburb of Awatuk a devoted wife and mother nursing a dying husband. The distance between that image and what a jury ultimately concluded she had done is the psychological chasm at the center of this story. She was born in 1970 and by the time the events that would define her unfolded, she was a woman in her early 30s with young children and a husband, Joe Andriano, who was gravely ill. Joe had been diagnosed with terminal cancer. To all appearances, Wendy was managing an unbearable situation with Grace, caring for a dying man, holding a family together, absorbing the strain that such a role imposes. The public sympathy that naturally flows toward a caregiver in that position was in her case part of the very cover behind which the crime took shape because beneath the surface, according to the case presented against her, the marriage was not what it seemed, and Wendy's private life was moving in a very different direction than her public role suggested. There were financial pressures. There was the matter of insurance. There were, prosecutors argued, personal entanglements outside the marriage. In the psychological portrait that emerged at trial, the strain of caregiving had not softened into devotion, but hardened into something colder. A calculation about escape, about money, and about a future she wanted that her husband's slow decline was not delivering quickly enough. On a night in October of 2000, Joe Andreano died, not from the cancer that had been expected to take him, but from violence. The medical and forensic evidence indicated that he had first been poisoned with a lethal substance, and that when the poison did not act as intended, the killing had been completed through a physical attack. The manner of his death transformed the case from a possible tragedy into a homicide investigation. Because the pattern of what had happened was inconsistent with any natural or accidental explanation. Wendy's account shifted and strained against the evidence. She offered explanations involving self-defense and a chaotic frightening confrontation. But the physical facts, the presence of poison, the sequence of events, the sheer effort involved in what had occurred were extraordinarily difficult to reconcile with the story she told. Investigators and later the jury were left to weigh the image of the loving caregiver against a body of evidence that pointed toward premeditation. Her defense at trial leaned heavily on her history and her psychology. Her attorneys presented an account of a troubled life, of abuse and trauma in her past, and argued for an understanding of her actions rooted in her emotional state and personal history. This is a recurring and genuinely difficult element in cases like hers. The reality that a person can be both a victim of earlier harm and the perpetrator of a later crime, and that the first truth does not erase the second. The jury was asked to hold both and in the end they concluded that whatever her history, the killing had been an intentional act. In 2004, Wendy Andriano was convicted of first-degree murder. The jury found the crime warranted the ultimate penalty and she was sentenced to death. She became one of the very small number of women on Arizona's death row and she has remained there through the years of appeals that inevitably follow such a sentence. With her legal team raising challenges, including questions about the effectiveness of her original defense, the psychological weight of her case comes from its intimacy. This was not a random attack by an outsider. It was a betrayal from within the most trusted relationship a dying man had, committed by the very person at his bedside. That kind of crime disturbs something deep in us because it turns the safest place, the home, the marriage, the sickbed vigil into the scene of the danger. What her story ultimately illustrates is how thoroughly a public role can conceal a private intention and how the sympathy we extend to caregivers, entirely appropriate in almost every case, can in the rarest instances become the perfect cover. Wendy Andriano's crime forced the community around her to confront how little they had truly seen of the woman they thought they knew. And that recognition is its own quiet horror. Number six, Robert Charles Comr. He asked to die. After 16 years on Arizona's death row, a man convicted of a brutal campsite murder made the deliberate choice to end his appeals and let the state carry out his sentence. And that decision, more than the crime itself, opens a window into the psychology of a man who had in some sense given up on his own existence long before the state ever intervened. Robert Comr is a study in a mind shaped by damage and finally exhausted by it. His early life, according to the records assembled by those who examined his case, was marked by profound instability and abuse. The kind of childhood that experts repeatedly encounter in the histories of violent offenders. It is worth restating the essential point. An abusive upbringing explains nothing on its own because countless people survive terrible childhoods and never harm another soul. But in the specific psychological chain that produced Robert Comr, that early damage appears to have fed a deep antisocial current, a hardened indifference to others that would eventually express itself in violence. By 1987, Comr had a criminal history and was living on the margins. In February of that year, he was camping in the rugged country near Apache Lake in the desert east of Phoenix together with his girlfriend at a neighboring campsite was another camper, a man named Larry Pritchard whom Kamur and his companion invited to join them. That invitation ended in Pritchard's murder. Comr killed him and then over the hours that followed committed a series of further violent crimes against other people in the area, including armed robbery and assaults against another couple he encountered. What the evidence and the court record describe is not a single explosive moment, but a sustained stretch of predatory violence, a man who once he had crossed into killing, continued to inflict harm on the people unlucky enough to be near him. The psychological reading of this is bleak. It suggests not a loss of control in a single instant, but a period in which the ordinary internal restraints that stop most people from harming others were simply absent. He was during those hours operating entirely without them. He was arrested and brought to trial. The proceedings themselves became notable for a disturbing episode. At his sentencing, questions arose about his physical and mental state in the courtroom, and the circumstances surrounding how he was brought before the judge to receive the death sentence would later feature in his appeals. He was convicted of firstdegree murder along with the other violent counts, and he was sentenced to death. Then came the long years on death row, and with them the slow revelation of the man's relationship to his own life. Robert Comr's legal appeals moved through the courts as they do for every capital case, raising issues about his trial and sentencing. But at a certain point, Comr himself intervened in a way that few condemned prisoners do. He declared that he wished to abandon his appeals entirely. He wanted the process to stop. He wanted the sentence carried out. This created a genuine legal and ethical dilemma because a court cannot simply accept a death row prisoner's request to die without first being satisfied that the person is mentally competent to make such a choice. That the decision is rational and voluntary rather than the product of despair, illness, or the crushing conditions of confinement itself. His case became entangled in exactly that question. Was a man choosing death from a place of sound mind? Or was he a person so damaged and so worn down that the wish to die was itself a symptom? Courts examined the question at length. In the end, his competence to make the decision was upheld, and in May of 2007, Robert Comr was executed by the state of Arizona. It was the first execution the state had carried out in several years. His case sits at an uncomfortable intersection of psychology and law. It forces a confrontation with the reality that the machinery of capital punishment can encounter a person who no longer resists it and that this absence of resistance does not simplify the moral questions but deepens them. Comr left behind no grand statement, no coherent explanation for the violence at Apache Lake. What he left was the image of a life that had been broken early, had broken others in turn, and had finally arrived at a kind of terminal indifference to its own continuation. That is perhaps the most desolate ending a human story can have. Number seven, Marjgery Anne Orbin. Investigators began with a torso and almost nothing else. A portion of a man's body discovered in the Arizona desert with no immediate way to know who he was or how he had come to be there. The path from that grim discovery back to a former Las Vegas showgirl living a suburban Phoenix life is one of the strangest and most revealing journeys in the state's criminal history. And it exposes a personality built almost entirely around reinvention and appetite. Marjgerie Orbin's life before the crime reads like a series of dramatic transformations. She had lived by her own accounts and those of others a colorful and mobile existence. a former dancer and performer, a woman who had moved through multiple marriages and identities, someone accustomed to remaking herself as circumstances demanded. By the early 2000s, she was married to Jay Orbin, a successful businessman who dealt in Native American art and jewelry, and who traveled frequently for his work. To the outside world, they were an established suburban couple with a young son. Beneath that surface, the marriage was under enormous strange strain. There were financial entanglements bound up in Jay's business and their shared life. There was, according to the case presented later, another relationship in Marjgery's life. The psychological portrait that emerged was of a woman who had spent her entire adult life arranging reality to suit her desires and who now found herself in a marriage she wanted to exit on terms that would preserve the lifestyle she had grown accustomed to. In 2004, Jay Orbin disappeared. He had been traveling for business, and when he failed to return as expected, the alarm was raised. Marjgery reported him missing. For a time, the case had the shape of an ordinary missing person inquiry. But investigators grew uneasy as inconsistencies accumulated. Questions about finances, about Jay's business accounts, about the timeline of his supposed movements. The story Marjgery told did not hold together under scrutiny. Then came the discovery in the desert. When the remains were eventually identified as Jay Orbin, the case transformed instantly from a disappearance into a homicide and the full weight of the investigation turned toward the wife who had reported him missing. What the evidence revealed was a killing followed by an elaborate effort at concealment, an attempt to make a man vanish and to sustain the fiction of his continued life through manipulation of his affairs. The prosecution's account placed the crime squarely within Marjgery's control, describing a killing carried out in the family home and a methodical, disturbing effort afterward to dispose of the evidence. Marjgery's defense sought to shift responsibility elsewhere, pointing toward the other man in her life and portraying herself as someone caught up in event driven by another. This became the central battleground of the trial. Not whether Jay had been murdered, which was undeniable, but who had done it and who had directed it. The jury weighed the competing narratives against the physical and financial evidence. In 2009, Marjgery Orbin was convicted of firstdegree murder. She was spared the death penalty and she was sentenced instead to life in prison where she remains. The psychological thread that runs through her case is the theme of reinvention taken to a lethal extreme. Here was a person whose entire life had been an exercise in becoming someone new whenever the old identity ceased to serve. A dancer, a wife again and again. In that light, the crime and its aftermath can be read as the ultimate expression of that pattern, the attempt to simply erase an inconvenient reality, to make a husband disappear and rewrite the story of her life around his absence. It was reinvention pursued past every moral boundary until the reshaping of reality required a body to be hidden in the desert. What her case leaves behind is a meditation on the danger of a self with no fixed truth. A personality so practiced at rearranging its own story that even the permanence of another person's life became in her mind just another detail to be edited. The desert kept its secret for only so long and when it gave the body back it gave back the truth along with it. Number eight, Samuel John Dietman. He was in a sense the follower rather than the leader. But the story of the serial shooter terror cannot be fully understood without the man who rode alongside the violence and then crucially was the one who broke. Samuel Dietman's psychology is that of a person drawn into another's darkness. And his case raises hard questions about weakness, complicity, and the moment a man decides to stop. Dyman's life before the shootings was, by the available accounts, unremarkable in the way that many lives on the margins are unremarkable. A man without much direction, struggling, drifting, and eventually falling into the orbit of Dale Howner, whose fixation on random violence has already been described. The relationship between the two men is central to understanding what happened because it appears to have been a dynamic in which one personality supplied the driving compulsion and the other supplied companionship, participation, and a kind of terrible validation. This is a wellocumented pattern in paired offenders. One partner is typically the dominant force, the source of the fantasy and the drive. The other is drawn in sometimes gradually until they have crossed lines. They might never have approached alone. That does not absolve the follower. Dietmen participated in lethal violence and bore full legal responsibility for it, but it does explain the psychology of how an otherwise directionless man became part of one of the most frightening crime sprees in the region's history. He found in Howner's company an escape from his own emptiness, and he followed that escape into murder. During the height of the spree in 2005 and 2006, Dietman took part in the random shootings that killed and wounded strangers across the Phoenix area. The attacks, as described earlier, had no rational motive and no pattern that could protect the public. For a time the two men moved through the city as predators, and the terror they created was indiscriminate. But Dietman had a weakness that Howner apparently did not, a conscience that could not be fully silenced, or at least a mouth that could not stay shut. He talked, he spoke about the crimes to an acquaintance, and that acquaintance, disturbed by what he heard, went to the authorities. This became the thread that unraveled the entire case. Surveillance was established and investigators built the evidence that led to the arrests in August of 2006. Once in custody, Dietman made the choice that would define his legacy in the case. He confessed and he cooperated. His account of the crimes and his willingness to testify became instrumental in the prosecution of Hner, the man the courts identified as the driving force behind the spree. In exchange for his cooperation, Dietman was spared the death penalty. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life in prison where he remains. The psychological interest in his case lies in the contrast between the two men. Howner pursued death and when convicted sought his own execution and ultimately took his own life. Dietman the follower chose survival and cooperation and in doing so helped bring the terror to an end. It is a reminder that even within a shared crime, two very different interior lives can be at work. One consumed entirely by the violence, the other never quite able to fully belong to it and finally turning against it. There is no redemption story here, and it would be wrong to construct one. Dietman participated in the taking of innocent lives, and nothing he did afterward can undo that. But his case illustrates a specific and important truth about paired violence. That the weaker partner, the one drawn in rather than driving, is often the point at which such a partnership can be broken. His confession did not make him a hero. It simply made him the crack in the structure through which justice finally reached both men. Number nine, Ernesto Arturo Miranda. His crime was serious, but his name became famous for something almost entirely detached from what he did to his victim. And that strange separation between the man and his legacy is what makes his case unlike any other on this list. To understand Ernesto Miranda is to understand how a single ordinary criminal through the accident of his case reaching the highest court in the land reshaped the relationship between every American and the police who might one day question them. Miranda's early life was marked by trouble from a young age. Born in 1941 in Mesa, Arizona, he struggled in school, lost his mother early, and had repeated encounters with the law throughout his adolescence. By the time he reached adulthood, he had accumulated a record and had spent time in custody in more than one state. He was, in the language of the era, a habitual petty offender whose trajectory had been pointing in a troubling direction for years. This was not a man with a hidden double life. His difficulties were visible and long-standing. In March of 1963 in Phoenix, Miranda was arrested in connection with the kidnapping and rape of a young woman. He was brought to the police station and questioned. During that interrogation, without being informed that he had the right to remain silent or the right to an attorney, he made statements and signed a written confession. That confession was central to the case against him. At his trial, it was presented to the jury and he was convicted of kidnapping and rape and sentenced to a lengthy prison term. For most defendants, the story would have ended there. But Miranda's conviction was appealed, and the appeal raised a question that reached far beyond his individual guilt. whether a confession obtained without informing a suspect of their constitutional rights could be used against them. The case climbed through the courts until it reached the Supreme Court of the United States, where it was decided in 1966 under the name that everyone now recognizes, Miranda versus Arizona. The court's ruling transformed American law enforcement. It held that suspects in custody must be informed of their rights before interrogation. The right to remain silent, the warning that anything said can be used against them, the right to an attorney, and the provision of one if they could not afford it. These became known as the Miranda warnings, and they are now recited so routinely in real life and in fiction that most people can repeat them from memory. Because his confession had been obtained without such warnings, Miranda's original conviction was overturned. It is important to be precise about what this did and did not mean. It did not mean Miranda went free. He was retrieded, this time without the tainted confession, and on the strength of other evidence he was convicted again and returned to prison. The ruling that bears his name protected a principle, not a person. The man himself remained, in the eyes of the law, guilty of a serious crime. The final chapter of his life carried a grim irony. After being released from prison years later, Miranda lived a marginal existence, and in 1976, he was killed in a bar fight in Phoenix. According to the accounts of the time, a suspect in his death was read the very warnings that bore Miranda's own name. Whether or not that detail has been polished by retelling, it captures the strange symmetry of a life whose greatest significance lay entirely outside the man's own intentions. The psychological and historical interest of his case is unusual because it is not really about the interior darkness of a killer. Miranda was a repeat offender, not a monster of the kind found elsewhere on this list. What makes his story matter is the way the American legal system took one flawed man's case and used it to draw a permanent line around the power of the state over the individual. His name outlived him and outgrew him entirely, attached now not to his crime, but to a protection that shields the guilty and innocent alike. Few criminals have ever left a mark so large and so completely. Number 10, Robert Henry Mormon. The crime that ended his life was not the crime that first put him behind bars, and the man he killed was not a stranger. It was the woman who had raised him. Robert Mormon's case is a disturbing study in a mind that was by the assessments made throughout his life genuinely impaired, and it forces the hardest questions about how the justice system should treat an offender whose intellectual and psychological deficits are as real as his guilt. Morman's history was troubled long before the killing that would define his final years. Born in 1948, he had a background that included documented intellectual limitations and psychological problems. And by the early 1980s, he was already incarcerated in the Arizona State Prison in Florence, serving a sentence connected to the kidnapping of a child years earlier. He was, in other words, a man already known to the system as dangerous and already assessed as impaired. In January of 1984, Morman was granted a compassionate furlow, a temporary release from prison to spend time with his adoptive mother, Roberta, who traveled to Florence to visit him. They stayed together at a small motel near the prison during the furlow. It was during this authorized release that the crime occurred. Morman killed Roberta, the woman who had adopted and raised him, and then committed acts against her body that were among the most disturbing details ever presented in an Arizonan courtroom. Out of respect, those specifics are left to the record. What followed revealed the strange, almost childlike quality of his thinking. Rather than fleeing, Mormon behaved in ways that quickly drew attention, including efforts to dispose of evidence that were clumsy and conspicuous, and interactions with local businesses that raised immediate alarm. The concealment was not the work of a calculating mind covering its tracks with skill. It was disorganized and self-defeating, consistent with the intellectual limitations that had followed him throughout his life. Investigators identified what had happened with little difficulty and Morman was arrested. He was convicted of firstdegree murder and sentenced to death. And here his case became part of one of the most significant ongoing debates in American criminal justice. The question of whether it is just to execute a person with serious intellectual disability. Over the years of his appeals, his lawyers argued extensively that his mental deficits should exempt him from the ultimate punishment, pointing to a lifetime of documented impairment. This was the same broad legal territory that produced major Supreme Court decisions limiting the execution of the intellectually disabled. In Morman's case, however, the courts ultimately concluded that his impairments, while real, did not meet the legal threshold that would bar his execution. His appeals were exhausted, and in February of 2012, Robert Mormon was executed by the state of Arizona. The psychological weight of his story lies in its terrible intimacy and in the discomfort it leaves behind. This was a man who killed the person who had chosen to be his mother during a moment of compassion extended to him by the very system that held him. It was a crime that combined profound personal betrayal with the mechanical failure of a decision to grant furlow to a man who should perhaps never have been released even briefly. and it ended with an execution carried out on a person whose mind by every assessment functioned well below that of an ordinary adult. There are no satisfying conclusions in a case like this. It offers no clean villain of the kind the imagination prefers and no comfortable moral resting place. It leaves instead a series of hard questions about responsibility, capacity, mercy, and punishment. questions that the law answered in one specific way and that continue to trouble anyone who examines the case closely. Robert Mormon's story is the quietest and least famous on this list and in some ways the most unsettling because it refuses to let us look away from the places where human damage and human justice meet. And neither one comes away clean. A note on sensitivity. Several of these cases touch on abuse, mental illness and suicide. Tội ác của anh ta rất nghiêm trọng nhưng tên tuổi của anh ta lại trở nên nổi tiếng vì một thứ gần như hoàn toàn tách biệt từ những gì hắn đã làm với nạn nhân của mình. Và sự tách biệt kỳ lạ giữa con người và di sản của anh ta chính là điều tạo nên trường hợp không giống bất kỳ trường hợp nào khác trong danh sách này. Hiểu Ernesto Miranda là hiểu cách một tên tội phạm bình thường thông qua tai nạn của vụ án của anh ta đạt tới tòa án cao nhất trong nước đã định hình lại mối quan hệ giữa mọi người Mỹ và cảnh sát, những người một ngày nào đó có thể thẩm vấn họ. Cuộc sống ban đầu của Miranda được đánh dấu bằng những rắc rối từ khi còn trẻ. Sinh năm 1941 tại Mesa, Arizona, ông học hành chật vật, mất mẹ sớm, và đã nhiều lần chạm trán với pháp luật trong suốt tuổi thiếu niên của mình. Khi đến tuổi trưởng thành, anh ấy đã tích lũy được một kỷ lục và chi tiêu thời gian bị giam giữ ở nhiều tiểu bang. Theo ngôn ngữ của thời đại, anh ta là một kẻ phạm tội nhỏ thường xuyên có quỹ đạo đã chỉ theo một hướng đáng lo ngại trong nhiều năm. Đây không phải là một người đàn ông có cuộc sống hai mặt ẩn giấu. Những khó khăn của anh ấy hiện rõ và tồn tại lâu dài. Vào tháng 3 năm 1963 tại Phoenix, Miranda bị bắt vì liên quan đến vụ bắt cóc và cưỡng hiếp một cô gái trẻ. Anh ta bị đưa đến đồn cảnh sát và bị thẩm vấn. Trong cuộc thẩm vấn đó, không được thông báo rằng anh ta có quyền giữ im lặng hoặc quyền có luật sư, anh ta đã khai báo và ký vào văn bản nhận tội. Lời thú nhận đó là trọng tâm của vụ án chống lại anh ta. Tại phiên tòa xét xử, nó đã được trình bày trước bồi thẩm đoàn và anh ta bị kết tội bắt cóc và hiếp dâm và bị kết án tù dài hạn. Đối với hầu hết các bị cáo, câu chuyện lẽ ra đã kết thúc ở đó. Nhưng bản án của Miranda đã bị kháng cáo và kháng cáo đã đặt ra một câu hỏi sâu rộng ngoài cảm giác tội lỗi của cá nhân anh ta. liệu lời thú tội có được mà không thông báo cho nghi phạm về các quyền hiến định của họ có thể là được sử dụng để chống lại họ. Vụ án leo thang qua các tòa án cho đến khi đến Tòa án tối cao của Hoa Kỳ, nơi nó được quyết định vào năm 1966 dưới cái tên mà mọi người bây giờ nhận ra, Miranda đấu với Arizona. Phán quyết của tòa án đã thay đổi việc thực thi pháp luật của Mỹ. Nó cho rằng nghi phạm bị giam giữ phải được thông báo về quyền của họ trước khi thẩm vấn. Quyền giữ im lặng, cảnh báo rằng bất cứ điều gì nói ra đều có thể được sử dụng để chống lại họ, quyền có luật sư và việc cung cấp luật sư nếu họ có thể không đủ khả năng. Những điều này được gọi là những lời cảnh báo Miranda, và giờ đây chúng được đọc lại thường xuyên trong đời thực và trong tiểu thuyết mà hầu hết mọi người đều có thể lặp lại chúng theo trí nhớ. Điều quan trọng là phải xác định chính xác điều này có ý nghĩa gì và không có ý nghĩa gì. Điều đó không có nghĩa là Miranda được tự do. Phán quyết mang tên ông bảo vệ một nguyên tắc chứ không phải một con người. Bản thân người đàn ông này, trước pháp luật, vẫn phạm tội nghiêm trọng tội phạm.
